title: How to Avoid Jumping to Conclusions: Measuring the Robustness of Outstanding Facts in Knowledge Graphs

problem.claim: Truthful outstanding facts can become misleading when lateral contexts and data that reduce their strikingness are ignored, creating risks for fairness and transparency.

gap.claim: Knowledge-graph mining lacks a capacity to inspect the robustness of outstanding facts against lateral contexts and relevant data.

contributions.claim: A perturbation-analysis methodology measures the robustness of outstanding facts in knowledge graphs.
The methodology includes entity perturbation for outlying contexts and data perturbation for plausible data that reduce an outstanding fact's strikingness.
The paper provides exact and sampling algorithms for perturbation analysis on large knowledge graphs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their methodology accurately and efficiently detects frail outstanding facts produced by existing knowledge-graph mining approaches.
The authors report effectiveness through case studies and user studies.

narrative_sequence.summary: Outstanding facts are striking claims about entities relative to peers and support journalism, fact checking, and recommendation.
Outstanding facts may appear persuasive when contextual information or less-striking plausible data are ignored, causing public, fairness, and transparency concerns.
Existing knowledge-graph mining lacks robustness inspection for outstanding facts.
The proposed approach uses entity and data perturbations, expected strikingness, and deviation-based robustness assessment.
Exact and sampling algorithms are evaluated in experiments, case studies, and user studies.

source_observation.claim: A fact's apparent significance can change when relevant contexts or plausible alternative data are considered.

interpretation.claim: Robustness assessment should test whether a conclusion remains striking under structured contextual and data perturbations.

application.claim: Use perturbation-based checks before presenting knowledge-graph-derived claims in journalism, fact checking, recommendation, or consequential decisions.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which perturbations are sufficient for every domain or claim type.

unknowns: No datasets, knowledge graphs, or experimental settings are specified.
No quantitative accuracy, efficiency, or robustness results are provided.
The perturbation relevance distributions and significance-deviation criteria are not detailed.
The case-study and user-study participants and procedures are unspecified.
No comparison details against existing mining or robustness methods are provided.
